focus: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness

items.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
items.source: Dao, Fu, Ermon, Rudra, Re (Stanford, NeurIPS 2022)
items.why: Attention is memory-bound, not FLOP-bound, and this paper is the cleanest demonstration of designing an algorithm around a memory hierarchy with a provable IO bound. The same reasoning (tile, fuse, recompute instead of store) applies to every GPU kernel you will ever read, and to CPU cache blocking and external-memory algorithms generally.
items.summary:
The paper starts from the hardware: an A100 has 40 to 80 GB of HBM at roughly 1.5 to 2 TB/s, but only about 192 KB of on-chip SRAM per streaming multiprocessor at roughly 19 TB/s. Softmax, masking and dropout are memory-bound, so the cost of standard attention is dominated by writing and re-reading the N by N score and probability matrices through HBM, not by the matmuls. Standard attention does Theta(Nd + N^2) HBM accesses.

FlashAttention computes exact attention without ever materializing the N by N matrix in HBM. It tiles Q, K and V into blocks sized from the SRAM budget (column block about M/4d), loops over K/V blocks in the outer loop and Q blocks in the inner loop, and fuses matmul, scaling, mask, softmax and the second matmul into one CUDA kernel. The enabling trick is online softmax: per row it keeps a running max m and running sum of exponentials l, and merges partial results from two blocks by rescaling with e^(m_old - m_new). That makes softmax decomposable across tiles while staying numerically stable. Extra memory is O(N).

The IO complexity is Theta(N^2 d^2 / M), which for typical head dimensions (64 to 128) and SRAM sizes is many times fewer HBM accesses than standard attention. The paper also proves that no exact algorithm can asymptotically beat this over all SRAM sizes.

The backward pass does not store the N by N matrices either. It saves the output and the softmax statistics, and recomputes scores and probabilities on-chip, which the authors call a form of selective gradient checkpointing. Recomputation raises FLOPs but cuts HBM traffic enough to win. Their GPT-2 medium measurement at sequence length 1024 on an A100 shows it: standard attention 66.6 GFLOPs, 40.3 GB of HBM reads and writes, 41.7 ms; FlashAttention 75.2 GFLOPs, 4.4 GB, 7.3 ms. More FLOPs, far less time.

A block-sparse variant skips zero blocks and has IO cost scaled by the fraction of nonzero blocks. End-to-end results: BERT-large training about 15 percent faster than the MLPerf 1.1 record, GPT-2 about 3x faster than common baselines, long-range arena about 2.4x, and enabling longer contexts improved GPT-2 perplexity and long-document classification. Read the 3x and 7.6x figures as different baselines and settings, not one number.
items.exercise: In Python with numpy (or PyTorch on CPU), implement tiled attention with online softmax: block over K/V, carry m and l per query row, and rescale the running output accumulator. Verify it matches naive softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d))V to 1e-6 for random inputs including large-magnitude logits that overflow a naive exp. Then count simulated 'HBM' reads and writes for both versions as a function of N, M and block size, and plot the crossover. Stretch: write the same loop as a Triton kernel and time it against torch scaled_dot_product_attention.

items.title: A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector
items.why: It is the best short treatment of GC as an explicit cost model rather than folklore. The CPU-versus-memory trade-off, the GOGC formula and the soft memory limit transfer directly to reasoning about .NET and JVM GC settings in containers, where OOM kills and GC thrashing are real production failure modes.
items.summary:
The guide builds a model from three axioms. Memory cost of a cycle is the live heap from the previous cycle plus the new heap allocated during it. CPU cost of a cycle is a fixed per-cycle cost plus a per-byte marking cost times the live heap found. Sweeping is ignored because it is negligible next to marking. A worked steady-state example: allocating 10 MiB/s with a 10 MiB live heap and a 100 MiB per cpu-second scan rate gives 10 percent GC CPU with 1 second cycles, and 5 percent with 2 second cycles at 50 percent more memory. So GC frequency trades CPU directly against memory.

GOGC controls that trade: target heap = live heap + (live heap + GC roots) x GOGC / 100, with roots counted since Go 1.18. Doubling GOGC roughly doubles heap overhead and roughly halves GC CPU. There is a 4 MiB minimum total heap target, and GOGC=off means an unbounded target.

The memory limit (GOMEMLIMIT or debug.SetMemoryLimit) is a soft cap measured as total runtime-mapped memory minus memory already released to the OS. As usage approaches it, the GC runs more often. To avoid the death spiral where the live heap nears the limit and GC runs continuously, the runtime caps GC CPU at about 50 percent over a window, so a misconfigured limit slows a program by at most about 2x instead of stalling it. Combining GOGC=off with a limit is a valid strategy, and the guide suggests leaving 5 to 10 percent headroom in containers. It also argues that failing fast with an OOM is often better than an indefinite stall.

On latency, the collector is concurrent and has no pause proportional to heap size, but latency still comes from five sources: brief stop-the-world transitions, GC taking about 25 percent of CPU during marking, mutator assists that tax allocating goroutines, write barriers, and stack scanning. Execution traces expose all of these except write barriers. The guide ends with practical diagnosis (gctrace, execution traces, heap profiles, escape analysis) and notes on finalizers versus cleanups. Note: I read the cost model, GOGC, memory limit, latency sections verbatim; the profiling thresholds near the end of the page were not independently verified, so check them on the page.
items.exercise: Write a small Go program with a controllable allocation rate and a fixed live heap (for example a map or slice of 50 MiB). Sweep GOGC over 25, 50, 100, 200, 400 and record GC CPU fraction (runtime/metrics) and peak RSS. Fit the guide's model to your measurements and see where it breaks. Then run it in a Docker container with a 256 MiB limit and compare GOMEMLIMIT unset, set at 90 percent, and set too low, observing OOM kill versus thrashing in gctrace output. Port the same experiment to .NET with DOTNET_GCgen0size or GCHeapHardLimit to compare behavior.

items.title: MonetDB/X100 - A DBMS In The CPU Cache
items.source: Zukowski, Boncz, Nes, Heman (CWI, IEEE Data Engineering Bulletin 2005)
items.why: Vectorized execution is the core idea behind DuckDB, ClickHouse, Velox, Snowflake and Photon. This paper explains why tuple-at-a-time Volcano is slow on modern CPUs, from first principles of instruction-level parallelism and caches, which is exactly the reasoning you need to evaluate any analytical engine. It is the companion to the better-known CIDR 2005 paper and covers the same system.
items.summary:
The motivating measurement is TPC-H Q1 at scale factor 1 with data in memory. Classic tuple-at-a-time engines take tens of seconds (28.1 s and 26.6 s for the two commercial and open-source systems listed), MonetDB/MIL takes 3.7 s, MonetDB/X100 takes 0.60 s, and hand-written C takes 0.22 s. The authors blame the Volcano iterator model: per-tuple interpretation overhead dominates, and the long dependency chains through virtual calls hide instruction-level parallelism, so IPC is low. A two-value multiply costs about 2 cycles per tuple in X100 versus about 49 in MySQL, per the paper's citation.

X100's fix is to process vectors, small aligned arrays of a few hundred to a few thousand values, through specialized primitives such as a map_mul primitive over two float columns with an optional selection vector. Each primitive is a tight loop with no per-tuple function calls, which the compiler can pipeline and unroll, so primitives reach IPC above 2 and cost on the order of 2 to 6 cycles per tuple (selection about 3, arithmetic about 2, sum aggregation about 6). Interpretation overhead is amortized over the whole vector.

Vector size matters. At size 1 you recover tuple-at-a-time performance. Growing the vector gains roughly two orders of magnitude until vectors stop fitting in cache, after which intermediate results spill to memory and performance degrades toward MonetDB/MIL, which materializes full columns. The design target is therefore vectors sized so all of a pipeline's intermediates live in L1 or L2.

Two refinements follow. Selection vectors carry the positions of qualifying tuples instead of copying survivors, avoiding materialization after filters. Compound primitives fuse a whole expression subtree into one loop to avoid the load and store of every intermediate vector, at the price of generating code (the paper has predefined ones and names JIT as a goal). On storage, the ColumnBM layer uses column-wise layout and ultra-lightweight compression with branch-free kernels, decompressing per vector between cache and memory. Query speedup tracks the compression ratio, roughly 3x bandwidth on TPC-H.
items.exercise: In C# (using Span<T> and System.Numerics.Vector<T>) or Rust, implement TPC-H Q1-style aggregation (filter, a few arithmetic expressions, group-by sum) over a few hundred MB of generated lineitem-like columns in three modes: row-at-a-time with virtual-call operators, column-at-a-time fully materialized, and vectorized with batch size as a parameter. Sweep batch size from 1 to 1M, plot time per tuple, and locate the L1/L2 cliff on your machine. Add a selection vector version and a fused expression version and report the delta.

items.title: Exactly-Once Semantics Are Possible: Here's How Apache Kafka Does It
items.source: Neha Narkhede and Guozhang Wang, Confluent
items.why: Exactly-once is one of the most misused phrases in data engineering. This post gives the precise scoping: what idempotence plus transactions actually guarantee inside a Kafka read-process-write loop, what they do not (external side effects), and what it costs. That distinction is the thing to carry into any pipeline you design.
items.summary:
The post separates two layers. The first is the idempotent producer, enabled with enable.idempotence=true, which gives exactly-once, in-order delivery per partition. The mechanism resembles TCP sequencing: each batch carries a sequence number and the broker drops duplicates caused by retries. Unlike TCP, the sequence information is persisted in the replicated log, so a newly elected leader after failover can still recognize a resend as a duplicate. Overhead is a few extra numeric fields per batch.

The second layer is transactions. A producer can write to multiple partitions atomically, so a batch is either visible to consumers or not at all, and consumer offsets can be committed inside the same transaction. That combination turns a read-process-write loop into an atomic unit, which is what makes end-to-end exactly-once work for stream processing. Each producer needs a stable transactional.id so state survives restarts, and a broker-side coordinator backed by an internal transaction log topic tracks transaction state. The post only sketches this and points to the design document for the protocol, so do not expect PID and epoch-fencing details here; KIP-98 is the place for that.

On the consumer side, isolation.level=read_committed hides records from open or aborted transactions, so consumers only see committed data, at the price of extra latency proportional to transaction duration. The post defines the stream-processing guarantee as each received record's results being reflected once even under failure, and is explicit that this covers Kafka-internal state and output, not side effects like calling an external API or database, which need an idempotent or transactional sink. Per the post's benchmarks, producer throughput drops roughly 3 percent for 1 KB messages with 100 ms transactions against a strict-ordering baseline, with larger penalties against a weaker baseline, and Kafka Streams loses 15 to 30 percent at a 100 ms commit interval but little at 30 seconds. Some of these figures came from a model-extracted portion of the page and should be checked against the post.
items.exercise: Using Docker Kafka (KRaft) and either Confluent.Kafka in C# or kafka-python, build a consume-transform-produce loop with transactions: read from topic A, write to topic B, and commit offsets with SendOffsetsToTransaction. Kill the process at randomized points (before commit, after produce but before commit) and verify with a read_committed consumer on B that no duplicates or losses appear, then repeat with plain at-least-once and count duplicates. Finally add an external side effect (writing to Postgres) and show where exactly-once breaks, then fix it with an idempotency key table.
